content:
Code discovered in iOS 27 beta suggests Apple may have built a system that can restrict leased devices when customers fall behind on payments. Here's what we found.

A little background

Bloomberg reported earlier that Apple is likely close to launching a new "Apple Upgrade" leasing program in the United States that lets customers purchase hardware with lower monthly payments.

According to the report, Apple is partnering with Klarna to provide financing for this program, covering most iPhone, Mac, iPad, and Apple Watch models. Reportedly, the lease term for iPhone and Apple Watch is 24 months, while Mac and iPad have a lease term of 36 months.

Bloomberg noted that customers can pay off the remaining balance before the lease term ends or upgrade to a newer model, with the latter potentially requiring an additional fee. At the end of the lease term, customers can either keep the device or return it, operating similarly to an auto lease.

What iOS 27 reveals

9to5Mac can now confirm that code discovered in the iOS 27 beta appears to reveal a broader system for managing financed iPhones, including the ability to restrict app and service functionality when customers default on payments.

The code describes a system called "App Managed Features," in which an authorized financing partner or vendor app can register an iPhone and continuously perform status checks.

If the contract status becomes abnormal, Apple's system services can place the iPhone into "Restricted Mode," blocking access to most apps until the payment or contract issue is resolved, with only a small number of apps remaining usable. The fixed whitelist currently found in the iOS 27 beta includes:

  • Accessibility Reader
  • App Store
  • Health
  • Magnifier
  • Phone
  • Clock
  • Settings
  • Wallet
  • Passwords
  • The Restricted Mode interface itself

Apps that can send important reminders (such as Messages, Home, and certain medication management or safety-related apps) may also remain available. However, vendors appear to have some control over these exceptions.

There is nothing in the code suggesting that App Store subscriptions tied to the restricted apps will be canceled, paused, or otherwise modified. Therefore, subscriptions may continue to be charged even while access to the relevant apps is restricted.

Additionally, there is no fixed number of missed payments that will automatically trigger these restrictions. When to lock the device is determined by the financing partner's app according to its own policies.

Finally, the new framework also introduces a new type of activation lock called "Partner Finance Lock," designed to prevent users from wiping, reselling, or disassembling restricted devices for parts.

This framework is built into Find My, but to be clear, financing partners do not have access to the device's location. The integration exists solely to maintain the finance lock even if the device is wiped or restored.

Given that Bloomberg reported Apple Upgrade launching next week, 9to5Mac already searched for the relevant code yesterday in the released iOS 26.6 RC, but did not find it. As a result, Apple will likely either add the necessary code to the final version of iOS 26.6 or postpone the Apple Upgrade launch.

Another point to note: the above findings are based on the current implementation of the framework in the iOS 27 beta, and some details may change before the official launch. However, the code references mentioned above do genuinely exist in the current code.

What are your thoughts on these findings? Feel free to share them in the comments.
